Photograph: Myanmar's Presidential Press and Information Bureau/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Aung San Suu Kyi with Arnaud de Baecque, resident representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross to Myanmar, in Naypyidaw. Photograph: Myanmar's Presidential Press and Information Bureau/AFP/Getty Images Myanmar Red Cross visits Aung San Suu Kyi after Myanmar military pushed to prove she is alive Meeting follows years of questions over wellbeing of detained former leader, who was ousted by coup in 2021 Natasha May in Bangkok Mon 3 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT First published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Myanmar’s detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi has met a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the aid organisation has confirmed. The meeting on Monday ⁠followed years of questions over the wellbeing of the 81-year-old , whose whereabouts and health condition have been largely unknown since the elected civilian government she led was ousted by a military coup in February 2021. Little has been seen or heard of Aung San Suu Kyi since late 2022 . Myanmar’s military-backed administrations have repeatedly claimed she is in “good health”, even as international pressure has grown on the country’s ​government to allow independent verification. Aung San Suu Kyi’s son, Kim Aris, who had recently demanded the ruling junta provide proof of life , welcomed news of the meeting. He described it as “the first positive development concerning her in more than five years”, adding: “This is an important first step, but it must not be the last,.” In a social media post, Aris said he hoped the meeting would lead to “greater humanitarian access, direct contact with my mother, credible and independently verified information about her wellbeing, and ultimately her immediate and unconditional release, together with all political prisoners”. Leaked footage and prison logs reveal Aung San Suu Kyi’s life in detention Read more On Monday, Arnaud de Baecque, the resident representative of the ICRC ​to Myanmar, visited Aung San Suu Kyi in the capital, Naypyidaw, the government spokesperson Khine Khine Soe said in a post on Telegram. View image in fullscreen Photo released by Myanmar’s government shows Aung San Suu Kyi cutting a birthday cake during her meeting with Arnaud de Baecque. Photograph: Myanmar President Office/AP In two of the four photographs provided by Khine Khine Soe, Aung San Suu Kyi – dressed in traditional ​Burmese attire – is seen with Baecque in a sparsely furnished, wood-panelled room containing only two chairs and a desk. In another photo, Myanmar’s former leader is seen cutting a birthday cake inscribed with her name. A clothes rack and storage boxes are visible in the background. A fourth image is a closeup of the cake, inscribed with “Happy Birthday Aunty Suu 19.6.2026”. In a statement released afterwards, the ICRC confirmed the visit had occurred and was carried out in accordance with its standards and procedures for visiting people deprived of liberty, including the opportunity to speak with Aung San Suu Kyi in private. “In line with the ICRC’s working methods, detention visits provide people deprived of liberty with the opportunity to exchange news with their families,” the statement said. “As is customary in the ICRC’s detention work, observations and recommendations related to the visit are shared exclusively and confidentially with the detaining authorities.” In late April, after a military-engineered election that allowed the former junta leader Min Aung ​Hlaing to become Myanmar’s ⁠president, authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi had been moved to house arrest. A photograph of the detained former leader was shown on military-controlled TV, however Aris told the BBC the image was taken years ago. While the election was largely criticised as a sham , it has led to diplomatic re-engagement with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean). ‘We feel like we are failing’: Myanmar doctor speaks out as health system teeters on ‘brink of collapse’ Read more Following a meeting between Myanmar’s foreign minister and counterparts from the regional Asean bloc in Bangkok in July, Thailand’s foreign minister, Sihasak Phuangketkeow, called for access to Aung San Suu Kyi “so that we can be able to verify the claims” of her good health. But the new military-backed administration had so far been reluctant to provide access ⁠to Aung San Suu ​Kyi, including a May request by the Philippines to allow an Asean special envoy to visit her. https://crisismagazine.com/opinion/stori.text: Stories From the Silver Screen: The Jeweler’s Shop The film "The Jeweler's Shop," based on the play written by Karol Wojtyla, the future Pope John Paul II, explores the meaning of marriage. Regis Martin PUBLISHED ON August 22, 2026 Part of a series about films so riveting that they deserve to be remembered long after they were first seen. Nearly five centuries of state sanctioned apostasy have passed since the death of Sir Thomas More, martyred for his faith in 1535, principally due to his steadfast defense of the sanctity of Christian marriage, for which defense Rome herself was prepared to suffer the loss of a unified Catholic Europe. But not everyone would sign on with the Protestant Revolt. The people of Poland, for instance, remained robustly, passionately Catholic. And it is there that our next story begins. It is the year 1939, the eve of the Second World War. Adolf Hitler and the armies of the Third Reich are about to march on Poland, which they will soon enough subject to brutal and protracted occupation, followed by the Soviets, whose occupation will prove even worse inasmuch as it will last far longer. It is against this awful backdrop of war that two young people meet, fall in love, and soon thereafter marry and have a family. But the husband will not survive. His life will be lost in defending the country that he loves. And except for the priest there at the end to administer the Last Rites, he will die alone, not knowing how the young child they conceived in love will grow up, forced to live without a father. Sir Thomas More, martyred for his faith in 1535, principally due to his steadfast defense of the sanctity of Christian marriage, for which defense Rome herself was prepared to suffer the loss of a unified Catholic Europe. Tweet This Welcome to The Jeweler’s Shop, a profound and beautiful movie based on a play written by Karol Wojtyla, who later became Pope St. John Paul II. Made in 1988, the film stars Burt Lancaster as the mysterious Jeweler who sells wedding rings to young couples while teaching them all that they will need to know about marriage and the sacrifices required to make it work. He does not actually sell anything, he only gives them freely away to couples willing to take on the burden, and the bliss, of what each ring represents. They cannot be returned. Not everyone will prove equal to the burden they have agreed to shoulder together. Some will require a great deal of remedial assistance. Yet grace is always there, freely dispensed for those who wish to begin anew—not once, but often and painfully. How does the poet Eliot put it? There is only the fight to recover what has been lost And found and lost again and again: and now, under conditions That seem unpropitious. But perhaps neither gain nor loss. For us, there is only the trying. The rest is not our business . That is because it is finally God’s business, who is certainly not above using human instruments to obtain his ends, consisting of nothing less than an eternity of happiness both with Him and in the company of those whom we are called upon to love. We do not go to Heaven alone. It is only in Hell that we find ourselves alone, endlessly telling God that we do not want to love or to be loved, only that we be left alone. Forever. The Jeweler thus stands for the durability, the indestructibility, of the marriage covenant into which couples are drawn, the working out of the choices they’ve made shown in every detail of the drama. Beginning with Andrew and Teresa, who, in the experience of their shared love, will find themselves face to face with the Jeweler, “his gaze at once gentle and penetrating…watching us while he was selecting and weighing the rings.” The future remains an unknown place, which they nevertheless “accept without anxiety. Love has overcome anxiety. The future depends on love.” Well, it had better be love on which the future—indeed, all life itself—will depend; because when circumstance conspires to undo the promises we have made, it will be love alone that enables us to endure. And it cannot be bought and sold like cheap flowers that soon wither away and die. “It has the taste of the whole man,” the Jeweler declares. It has his weight. And the weight of his whole fate. It cannot be a single moment. Man’s eternity passes through it. That is why it is to be found in the dimensions of God, because only He is eternity. It is a hard lesson, and for Teresa it must be learned early on, owing to Andrew’s untimely death at the front. And yet, as the priest strangely reveals on bringing her the news, “Your husband is more alive now than ever before.” And she believes him, knowing that this is the hope on which her life must now depend. “Andrew did not die in me,” she says, “did not die on any front, he did not even have to come back, for somehow he is.” In fact, he remains present in the child they had together, a son named Christopher, whom God had given them as the fruit of their shared love. And Christopher grew —and more and more I saw you (Andrew) in him. So I did not leave the sphere of your most strange person to whom I had given myself, from whom I do not know how to withdraw. Nor will she ever need to withdraw. Because, by God’s decree, we go with the dead even as they return to us, the two joined as one in Christ. “We die with the dying,” as Eliot reminds us in the last movement of Four Quartets : See, they depart, and we go with them. We are born with the dead: See, they return, and bring us with them. The moment of the rose and the moment of the yew-tree Are of equal duration. A people without history Is not redeemed from time, for history is a pattern Of timeless moments. How skillfully the film has stitched together such moments, allowing us to see the pattern, a veritable web of grace. But, alas, not all the couples shown will radiate that same intensity of attention intended by the sacrament to impart. Some will resist and, in their seeming refusal to recognize the Bridegroom in each other, will imperil not only their marriages but their very selves. Anna, for example, whose marriage to Stefan will soon unravel owing to his growing indifference. And the wound inflicted can never heal so long as he chooses not to feel her pain, “thinking, no doubt,” as she bitterly puts it, “she will get over it. Besides, he was confident of his rights, whereas I wanted him to win them continually. I did not want to feel like an object that cannot be lost once it has been acquired.” He, too, must learn to see, to awaken afresh to the realization that Anna, the woman he has callously taken for granted, must be rediscovered lest he lose both her and his soul—that only in her, this finite being given to him to love in a finite world, will he find an analogue adequate to those infinite longings he has, which we all have. It is the thirst for God that most deeply defines us, for God is a love that never ends. Indeed, His very being is love, eternal and triune. Which is why we find ourselves constantly on the lookout for images of this love in others—in order that somehow, in time, they might reflect something of the timeless countenance of Almighty God, which is the Face of the Bridegroom we were all created to see, to be embraced by for all eternity. Will they once again find this love in one another? Will the children of the two couples, who eventually meet and fall in love, will they succeed in keeping their love alive? Only by the grace of God, for which we are all beggars. Author Regis Martin Regis Martin is Professor of Theology and Faculty Associate with the Veritas Center for Ethics in Public Life at the Franciscan University of Steubenville. He earned a licentiate and a doctorate in sacred theology from the Pontifical University of St. Thomas Aquinas in Rome. Martin is the author of a number of books, including Still Point: Loss, Longing, and Our Search for God (2012) and The Beggar's Banquet (Emmaus Road). His most recent book, published by Sophia Institute Press, is March to Martyrdom: Seven Letters on Sanctity from St. Ignatius of Antioch . Orthodox. Faithful. Free. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c63d.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Greenlanders protested against Trump's ambitions for the territory in the country's capital, Nuuk, earlier this year By Oliver O'Connell ,Â Max Matza Â and Â Adrienne Murray ,Â Reporting from Copenhagen Published 18 September 2026 Updated 3 hours ago The US and Denmark have announced a deal on Greenland's security, resolving a diplomatic dispute sparked by President Donald Trump's threats to seize it by force. Nato said the deal would help stabilise the region, as Trump said Denmark would grant the US "permanent control over security, and all other needs" in the semi-autonomous Danish territory. The leaders of Denmark and Greenland welcomed the deal to "strengthen security", which they said was expected to be signed next week, but did not outline its contents. The deal comes after months of threats by Trump to "take" Greenland over national security concerns, citing its strategic location for defence purposes and its mineral wealth. No text of the agreement has been released. Trump said the deal came with "no cost to the United States" and would grant it the ability "to do what is necessary" to "secure and defend the security of Greenland", in a post on Truth Social. He said it included a rule that no US adversary could maintain a military presence in Greenland or "make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval". A Nato spokesperson said the military alliance welcomed the deal, which would "help advance security, stability and cooperation in this vital region". Denmark's Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement" for all three parties, which was expected to be signed at the UN General Assembly next week. The deal "strengthens our common security in the Arctic and the North Atlantic area" while also recognising "the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Kingdom and the right of the Greenlandic people to self-determination", she said in a joint statement with Greenland's Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen. The agreement would still need to go through "the necessary parliamentary procedures to enter into force" once signed, the statement noted. Nielsen said it was "gratifying that we are about to enter into an agreement that ensures and strengthens the security of Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark, the United States and the Western alliance". "The agreement recognises Greenland's interests and our place in international co-operation. It is for the benefit of us all," he said. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, US Vice-President JD Vance toured a US military base in Greenland earlier this year, in a visit viewed by Copenhagen and Nuuk as a provocation amid Trump's demands Trump had tried for months to purchase or annex the semi-autonomous territory, arguing that it was vulnerable to adversaries, including Russia and China. His repeated demands to take Greenland earlier this year prompted an outcry from Greenlanders, Danes and other Nato members. There is hope the crisis has now been brought to an end, with some Danish media interpreting the agreement as a quiet but significant triumph for the country's diplomacy. "Don't tell Trump that it's the Kingdom of Denmark that has won," read one headline in the newspaper Berlingske on Saturday. "Trump didn't get Greenland, but he was allowed to take a victory lap on social media," wrote a US correspondent for Politiken. Territorial integrity was a red line for Denmark and Greenland, and the US president has made no mention of any territory changing hands. It is not yet clear what concessions or sweeteners, if any, have been agreed - and in Greenland, some are still nervous. "[It's] news we have all been hoping for," MP Naaja Nathanielsen wrote on social media. But she added: "It is absolutely crucial that any agreement preserves our right to self-determination." Former Greenlandic politician Aaja Chemnitz said she looked forward to the deal being finalised, but "until then, I'm sceptical". "I don't have much confidence in Trump," she said. Image caption, Greenland's location between North America and the Arctic makes it well placed for early warning systems for missile attacks, and for monitoring vessels The text of the agreement has not been published. The BBC has contacted the Danish Embassy in the US and the White House. However, an unnamed US State Department official outlined the deal without providing specifics. Among the agreed provisions is one stating the deal would not expire even if Greenland became an independent country in the future. The official added that under the deal, the US has unilateral power to build additional military structures with no approval needed from Greenland or Denmark. It includes "permanent access, basing and overflights rights," the official said. It also bans non-Nato countries from building bases in Greenland, and "bans adversaries from making investments in Greenland that could threaten the United States". The official added that under the current status quo, adversaries have been allowed to invest in Greenland's "sensitive sectors without investment screening". The official specifically referenced Russia and China, saying it blocks them from deploying troops or making investments in "sensitive sectors". Without the official text being released, it is unclear how exactly the deal differs from a 1951 agreement with Denmark, under which the US can send as many troops as it wants to Greenland. The US already has more than 100 military personnel permanently stationed at its Pituffik base in the north-western tip of the territory. Trump says Greenland is essential for his plan to build a Golden Dome defence system, designed to protect the US against missile attacks from Russia and China, and that European allies could co-operate in this endeavour. The island has vast - and largely untapped - reserves of rare earth minerals, many of which are crucial for technologies including mobile phones and electric vehicles. Photograph: James Ross/AAP Business As tobacconist firebombings intensify in Melbourne, nearby stores are being denied insurance Arson attacks related to illegal tobacco trade are also causing revenue and reputation problems for neighbouring businesses Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Jonathan Barrett Business editor Sat 19 Sep 2026 16.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 22.33 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Small businesses located near tobacconists are being denied insurance or priced out of coverage as rising arson attacks turn neighbouring shops into collateral damage. The problem has intensified after a spate of firebombings, which includes a recent Melbourne blaze that destroyed a Richmond tobacco retailer and nearly a dozen neighbouring shops, requiring 80 firefighters to contain. Crime syndicates have been implicated in more than 200 firebombings of commercial and residential premises in Australia since 2023, according to government data, as rival groups vie for control of the illicit tobacco market. A Melbourne retailer, who asked not to be identified, told Guardian Australia their insurer refused to renew a policy because they were a “few doors down” from a tobacconist. “Even if we re-located, which is not really an option for us, who’s to say a tobacconist doesn’t move in next door?” the retailer said. The retailer said they’d received quotes from other insurers that don’t include fire cover. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Legitimate tobacconists have also reportedly been targeted by syndicates expanding their revenue base , making it difficult for them to secure coverage as well. The chief executive of the Council of Small Business Organisations Australia, Skye Cappuccio, said accessing or affording insurance for businesses located near tobacconists was becoming problematic. “Small businesses should not be left carrying the financial consequences of criminal activity that is beyond their control,” Cappuccio said. “We need a comprehensive effort from governments, law enforcement and regulators to address the illicit tobacco market, alongside broader action to address rising insurance costs and access to affordable cover for small businesses.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Big tobacco is back in town as cigarette tax fight lights up Australian politics Read more Small businesses close to tobacco market-related firebombings are also affected by loss of foot traffic, revenue and reputation, according to the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission. While insurers have not disclosed what constitutes “close proximity”, brokers generally consider it to be within about 20 metres of a tobacconist. Tobacco retailers within shopping complexes are seen as a lower risk. Illicit tobacco accounted for 80% of the cigarettes smoked by Australians in 2025 , according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, with untaxed packets costing as little as $10 compared with more than $40 for a legal packet. The surge in demand has sparked a political debate over whether Australia should reduce the tobacco excise to make legal cigarettes cheaper in order to curb illegal sales. Health experts have called for a focus on enforcement, which includes intercepting illegal products that enter the country through Australia’s ports. A spokesperson at Suncorp said the insurer no longer offered insurance cover for tobacconist retailers, including renewals for existing customers. The representative said businesses located near tobacconists may still be eligible, with underwriting decisions based on a range of factors, including the nature of the business and location-specific risks. “As with all commercial insurance, applications are considered on a case-by-case basis,” the spokesperson said. A QBE spokesperson said decisions were assessed individually. “Where risk profiles change, this can influence the price, terms or availability of cover,” the spokesperson said. http://en.people.cn/n3/2026/0910/c90000-.text: Home Opinion PD Voice Politics Foreign Affairs Business World We Are China Society Culture Sci-Tech Video Photo Sports Travel Military Life Exclusive Specials Languages Chinese Japanese French Spanish Russian Arabic Korean German Portuguese Swahili Italian Kazakh Thai Malay Greek Vietnamese Urdu Hindi Archive Global AI experts explore governance, innovation, applications at Budapest summit People pose for photo with a humanoid robot at the AI Summit Budapest 2026 in Budapest, Hungary on Sept. 7, 2026. (Photo by Attila Volgyi/Xinhua) Hungary's Minister of Science and Technology Zoltan Tanacs said AI can be "salvation or total catastrophe," stressing that governments should embrace innovation while putting appropriate safeguards in place as AI capabilities advance. BUDAPEST, Sept. 9 (Xinhua) -- Policymakers, researchers and industry leaders gathered at AI Summit Budapest 2026 on Monday and Tuesday to discuss artificial intelligence (AI) development, governance and applications as the technology rapidly reshapes economies and societies. The two-day summit brought together more than 300 speakers for discussions ranging from frontier AI models and digital infrastructure to governance and practical applications. Opening the summit, Hungary's Minister of Science and Technology Zoltan Tanacs described AI as a technology that lies "between two extremes" -- "salvation or total catastrophe." He said governments should embrace innovation while putting appropriate safeguards in place as AI capabilities advance. As part of its AI strategy, Hungary plans to invest 500 million euros (581.2 U.S. dollars) in AI development programs over the coming years and join the European AI Gigafactory initiative, which aims to strengthen Europe's AI computing infrastructure. Tanacs said Hungary also plans to expand AI education and university research, attract leading AI developers and improve AI literacy among businesses and the public. Addressing participants via video, Jin Xiaoming, president of the China Association for International Science and Technology Cooperation, warned that unequal access to AI technology and governance could widen what he called the "innovation divide." People attend the AI Summit Budapest 2026 in Budapest, Hungary on Sept. 7, 2026. (Photo by Attila Volgyi/Xinhua) "The gap between frontier AI creators and mere consumers keeps widening," Jin said, warning against "rules imposed by the few upon the many" and calling for AI governance based on shared responsibility, adaptive safeguards and human-centered development. The summit also explored the growing use of AI in business and industry. Presenting Alibaba Cloud's latest AI developments, Huang Ye, general manager of Solution and Products at Alibaba Cloud Central Europe, said AI is evolving from simply understanding users' requests to completing increasingly complex tasks and end-to-end workflows. Huang highlighted advances in model capabilities, human-AI collaboration and multimodal AI, as well as the growing role of open-source development. He said Alibaba Cloud has open-sourced more than 400 AI models, with more derivative models based on Qwen being used in areas such as education, healthcare and manufacturing. Huang said Alibaba Cloud was already using AI to improve customer service and assist engineers with coding and product demonstrations. People look at a humanoid robot at the AI Summit Budapest 2026 in Budapest, Hungary on Sept. 7, 2026. (Photo by Attila Volgyi/Xinhua) While opinions differed on how AI should develop and how it should be regulated, participants broadly agreed that closer international cooperation and wider access to AI technologies will be essential to ensuring that the technology benefits society. The fourth edition of the summit was held across three venues with 15 parallel tracks, bringing together nearly 4,000 attendees.
